Cardiology and hematology · published research

Thrombocytopenia

PBM increased platelet production in several mouse models, and a human-cell experiment found improved megakaryocyte maturation and platelet formation. No patient has received PBM for thrombocytopenia in the identified studies.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

Experimental findings consistently favor increased platelet production across immune-, radiation-, and chemotherapy-associated models. The evidence remains preclinical because the only human-derived work irradiated cell cultures rather than patients.

Summary of the Evidence

PBM increased platelet production and improved selected bleeding-related measures in mouse models. A human-cell ex-vivo study also reported improved megakaryocyte maturation and platelet formation in the presence of immune-thrombocytopenia plasma. No participant received PBM, so a clinical treatment effect remains unknown.

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical treatment study in people with thrombocytopenia was identified. Human umbilical-cord CD34-positive cell cultures were exposed to immune-thrombocytopenia plasma or platelet-targeting antibodies. PBM improved megakaryocyte maturation, proplatelet formation, and platelet production in this laboratory model (Wang et al. 2024).

Animal evidence

In mouse models, whole-body light exposure increased platelet production in immune-mediated, irradiation-related, and chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia. The 2016 studies reported improved platelet generation and model-specific bleeding measures, while Wang et al. linked the chemotherapy model to increased liver thrombopoietin and platelet production. These are separate experiments, but the two 2016 papers share a research line and should not be treated as independent clinical replication (Zhang et al. 2016; Yang et al. 2016; Wang et al. 2021).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Cell experiments in the animal papers examine megakaryocyte development and platelet formation. The ex-vivo human-cell work adds a human biological system, while the mouse study reports increased hepatic thrombopoietin through ROS-dependent Src/ERK/STAT3 signaling.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols differ. The mouse studies used whole-body red light around 635 nm or near-infrared light around 810–830 nm, with reported fluences around 23–36 J/cm² and repeated exposure. In visible terms, 635 nm is red; 810–830 nm is invisible near-infrared. The human-cell study irradiated cultures rather than a person. There is no patient-tested dose, route, or schedule and no head-to-head dose-finding study.

Interpretation

PBM affected thrombopoiesis in several experimental systems, including one using human cells and patient plasma. The results are favorable within these models, but they do not establish platelet recovery, bleeding benefit, or safety after PBM treatment in patients.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for platelet recovery in people with thrombocytopenia.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

No patient received PBM. The evidence consists of three mouse publications and one ex-vivo human-cell study using surrogate platelet-production outcomes. The two 2016 publications come from the same research group, and the models span different causes of thrombocytopenia.
